1.word_for_word: caturthe — in the fourth chapter; caṇḍikā-vākyam ākarṇya — hearing Caṇḍikā’s words; ati-bhaya-ākulaḥ — overwhelmed by extreme fear; durmantribhiḥ — through evil counselors; hitam mene — he considered beneficial; kaṁsaḥ — Kaṁsa; bāla-ādi-hiṁsanam — the killing of children and others.
1.translation: In the fourth chapter Kaṁsa, overwhelmed with fear after hearing Caṇḍikā’s words, accepts the evil advice of his wicked counselors and regards the killing of children and others as beneficial.

2.word_for_word: tat — that; aṣṭamam janma — the eighth birth.

6.word_for_word: aṅga — O dear one; he bhrātaḥ — O brother.

7.word_for_word: dīna-dīnavat — appearing even more pitiable than one who is truly pitiable; na tu tathā — though she was not actually so; putrasya anyatra nītatvāt — because her son had been taken elsewhere; sā ca yogamāyā iti jñātatvāt — and because she knew the girl to be Yogamāyā; yācitaḥ api — although he had been entreated; ācicchide — he tore her away; hastāt ākṛṣya jagrāha — pulling her from Devakī’s hands, he seized her.
7.translation: Devakī appeared even more wretched than a truly wretched person, although inwardly she knew that her son had been taken elsewhere and that this girl was Yogamāyā. Even after being entreated, Kaṁsa tore the child from her hands and seized her.

8.word_for_word: apothayat — he dashed or threw; balena — forcibly; cikṣepa — he hurled her.
8.translation: ‘Apothayat’ means that he forcibly hurled the child down.

9.word_for_word: sadyaḥ eva — immediately; devī bhūtvā — becoming the Goddess.
9.translation: She immediately assumed the form of the Goddess. Śrīdhara’s brief gloss covers verses 9–10.

10-11.word_for_word: sadyaḥ eva devī bhūtvā — immediately becoming the Goddess; 10 — the same gloss continues through verse 10; 11 — na vyākhyātam, not explained.
10-11.translation: Śrīdhara’s gloss on verses 9–10 is simply that she immediately became the Goddess. He gives no separate explanation for verse 11.

12.word_for_word: kṛpaṇān — the helpless ones; anyān śiśūn — the other children; haniṣyati iti jñātvā — knowing that Kaṁsa would kill them; vārayati — she restrains him; pāṭhāntare — in another reading; mā mām kṛpaṇām vṛthā ahiṁsīḥ — ‘do not uselessly harm me, a helpless woman’; hiṁsitavān asi — ‘you have already harmed me.’
12.translation: Knowing that Kaṁsa would otherwise kill other helpless children, the Goddess warns him not to do so. Śrīdhara also notes another reading in which she says, ‘Do not uselessly harm me, a helpless woman; you have already caused me suffering.’

13.word_for_word: bahu-nāma-niketeṣu — in abodes known by many names; vārāṇasī-ādi-sthāneṣu — in places such as Vārāṇasī.
13.translation: ‘In abodes of many names’ means in places such as Vārāṇasī.

14.word_for_word: parama-vismitaḥ — greatly astonished; katham — how?; daivī vāk — the divine prophecy; anṛtā jātā — has proved false.
14.translation: Kaṁsa was greatly astonished, wondering how the divine prophecy could apparently have proved false.

15.word_for_word: bhāma — O husband of my sister; he bhaginī-bhartaḥ — O brother-in-law; puruṣādaḥ — a man-eating Rākṣasa; yathā sva-apatyam eva hinasti — just as such a demon kills even his own offspring; tadvat — in the same way.
15.translation: ‘Bhāma’ addresses Vasudeva as the husband of Kaṁsa’s sister. Kaṁsa compares himself to a man-eating Rākṣasa who destroys even his own offspring.

18.word_for_word: he mahā-bhāgau — O greatly fortunate pair; sva-kṛtam bhujaḥ — those who experience the results of their own deeds; sva-ārabdha-karma-bhoktṝn — experiencers of the karma they themselves have begun; sva-ātmajān mā śocatam — do not grieve for your children; jantavaḥ prāṇinaḥ — living beings; sadā na āsate — do not remain forever; alpa-kālam eva — only for a short time; ekatra na āsate — they do not remain together in one place; viyujyante — they become separated; daiva-adhīnāḥ — being subject to destiny.
18.translation: O greatly fortunate pair, do not grieve for your children, who experience the results of their own previous actions. Living beings do not remain forever; they stay only briefly, and even then they do not remain together but are separated, because they are subject to destiny.

19.word_for_word: janma-maraṇa-ādi — birth, death and the like; dehānām eva — belong only to bodies; na ātmanaḥ — not to the Self; bhūtāni dehāḥ eva — ‘beings’ here means bodies; yānti apayānti ca — they come and go; bhavanti na bhavanti ca — they arise and cease; yathā bhuvi bhaumāni ghaṭa-ādīni — like earthen pots and other objects upon the earth; eṣu bhūteṣu vikriyamāṇeṣu — while these bodies undergo changes; ayam ātmā — this Self; aparokṣatayā pratyabhijñāyamānaḥ — directly recognized as the same self; na viparyeti — does not undergo alteration; eka-rūpaḥ eva vartate — remains of one nature; yathā bhūḥ — just as the earth remains while earthen things change; na śoka-ādi-avakāśaḥ — therefore there is no basis for grief and the like.
19.translation: The birth and death just mentioned belong to bodies, not to the Self. Bodies arise and disappear just as earthen pots and other objects come and go upon the earth. While bodies undergo such changes, the Self, directly recognized as the same ‘I,’ does not change but remains of one nature, just as the earth remains while earthen objects are transformed. Understood in this way, there is no basis for grief.

20.word_for_word: ajñānataḥ — because of ignorance; na nivartate — transmigration does not cease; anevam-vit — one who does not know matters as they really are; ātma-viparyayaḥ — mistaken conception of the Self; deha-ātma-buddhiḥ — identification of the body as the Self; tataḥ bhedaḥ — from that error comes division; deha-ahaṅkāreṇa — through bodily ego; ātmani paricchinne sati — when the Self is imagined to be limited; idam-kāra-āspadam bhinnam bhavati — the sphere of ‘this’ is conceived as separate; putra-ādi-dehaiḥ yogaḥ viyogaḥ ca — union and separation with the bodies of children and others; tataḥ saṁsṛtiḥ sukha-duḥkhe — from that come saṁsāra, happiness and suffering; yāvat ajñānam na nivartate — for as long as ignorance is not removed.
20.translation: Transmigration does not cease while ignorance remains. One who does not know the Self as it is identifies the body with the Self, and from that error comes the perception of separateness. When the Self is imagined to be limited by bodily ego, other bodies—children and the rest—appear separate, producing union and separation and consequently the happiness and sorrow of saṁsāra. This continues as long as ignorance is not removed.

21.word_for_word: na ete tava tanayāḥ — in truth these are not ultimately ‘your’ children; aham tu na ghātitavān — nor, ultimately, am I the killer; tathā api ajñāna-dṛṣṭyā — nevertheless, from the standpoint of ignorance; sva-tanayān mayā vyāpāditān api — your own children killed by me; mā anuśoca — do not grieve; sāntvayati — thus he consoles her; ajñāna-āśrayam eva karma-vādam āha — he then states the doctrine of karma at the level conditioned by ignorance.
21.translation: Kaṁsa consoles her by saying that, ultimately, these are not truly ‘your’ children and he is not the killer in relation to the Self. Yet even from the ordinary standpoint of ignorance, he says, ‘Do not grieve for your children killed by me.’ He then invokes the law of karma, which operates for those situated in ignorance.

22.word_for_word: brāhmaṇa-ādi-hantuḥ — for the killer of a brāhmaṇa and the like; tad-vadhyasya ca — and for the person killed; prāyaścitta-śravaṇam — scriptural injunctions of expiation; ajñāna-mūlam eva — have ignorance as their basis; asva-dṛk — one who does not see the true Self; deha-abhimānī — one identified with the body; tat-abhimānī — identifying with that body; tasya dehasya hananam ātmani abhimanyamānaḥ — imagining the body’s killing to be killing of the Self.
22.translation: If the Self is not truly killed, why do scriptures prescribe expiation for killing a brāhmaṇa and other persons? Śrīdhara answers that such injunctions operate within ignorance. ‘Asva-dṛk’ is one who does not see the true Self but identifies with the body, imagining the destruction of the body to be the destruction of the Self.

23.word_for_word: śyālaḥ — the brother-in-law; kaṁsaḥ — Kaṁsa; svasroḥ — literally ‘of the two sisters,’ an unusual dual; sva-sṛ-śabdena dvi-vacana-anupapattyā — because the dual does not fit the literal word ‘sister’; mithuna-lakṣaṇayā — by a secondary usage denoting the pair; svasṛ-tat-patyoḥ abhidhānam — the sister and her husband are intended; devakī-vasudevayoḥ pratyekam pādam agrahīt — he grasped one foot of Devakī and one of Vasudeva; śyāla-śabdena vā kathaṁcit vasudeva-abhidhānam — alternatively the word may in some way indicate Vasudeva’s relation as brother-in-law.
23.translation: Śrīdhara explains the unusual dual expression by taking it to denote the married pair: Kaṁsa, their brother-in-law, grasped the feet of both Devakī and Vasudeva—one foot of each—as he begged forgiveness.

24.word_for_word: ātma-sauhṛdam — his supposed friendship and goodwill; priya-vāda-ādinā — by pleasant speech and similar gestures; darśayan — displaying it.
24.translation: He displayed his supposed goodwill toward them through pleasant speech and similar gestures.

27.word_for_word: sva-para-bheda-darśane kim bhavati — what results from seeing the distinction of ‘mine’ and ‘other’?; śoka-harṣa-ādi-bhāvaiḥ — by states such as grief and joy; nimitta-bhūtaiḥ — functioning as immediate causes; mithaḥ bhāvān ghnantam — causing beings mutually to strike one another; bhāvam īśvaram — the underlying Reality, the Lord; pṛthag-dṛśaḥ na paśyanti — those who see separateness do not perceive Him; aham eva hantā hataḥ ca — instead they think ‘I am the killer’ and ‘I am killed.’
27.translation: What follows from seeing reality in terms of ‘mine’ and ‘other’? Those who see separateness are driven by states such as grief, joy, fear, hatred and greed and see beings as mutually killing one another. They fail to perceive the underlying Lord who governs these states, and instead think, ‘I am the killer’ or ‘I am the one killed.’

28.word_for_word: viśuddham — purely, without resentment; yathā bhavati — in a manner free from impurity.
28.translation: ‘Viśuddham’ means that Devakī and Vasudeva replied to him purely, without resentment.

29.word_for_word: na ati-kovidāḥ — not very wise; dṛṣṭa-mātra-matayaḥ — whose judgment extends only to what is immediately seen; na dīrgha-darśanāḥ — not farsighted.
29.translation: The demonic counselors were not truly wise: their judgment went no farther than what lay immediately before them, and they had no farsighted understanding.

30.word_for_word: na ati-kovidāḥ — not very wise; dṛṣṭa-mātra-matayaḥ — judging only by what was immediately visible; na dīrgha-darśanāḥ — not farsighted.
30.translation: ‘Not very wise’ means that they judged only by immediate appearances and lacked farsighted understanding.

31.word_for_word: anirdaśān — those for whom ten days have not passed; na nirgatāni daśa dināni yeṣām — infants not yet ten days old; anyān ca — and the others; nirdaśān — those who have reached ten days.
31.translation: ‘Anirdaśān’ means infants for whom ten days have not yet passed; the following expression includes those who have reached ten days.

33.word_for_word: asyataḥ — while shooting; vidhyataḥ sataḥ — while piercing them with arrows; utsṛjya — abandoning; raṇam tyaktvā — leaving the battle; palāyana-parāḥ — intent on flight.
33.translation: ‘Asyataḥ’ means while you were shooting and piercing them with arrows; ‘utsṛjya’ means that they abandoned the battlefield and fled.

35.word_for_word: anya-āsaktān — those engaged elsewhere; vimukhān ca — those whose backs are turned; na haṁsi — you do not kill; na hinatsi — you do not strike them down.
35.translation: You do not kill those who are occupied elsewhere or have turned away from battle.

36.word_for_word: kṣeme — in a safe place; nirbhaye deśe — in a place free from danger; śūraiḥ — heroes; saṁyugāt anyatra — away from battle; vikatthanam — boasting; prauḍhi-vādaḥ — swaggering claims of prowess; yeṣām — whose; harer bibhemi śambhoḥ ca — ‘But I fear Hari and Śambhu’; rahas-juṣā hariṇā — Hari who remains hidden; sarvasya antaḥ-praviṣṭena — having entered within everyone; kvacit api bahiḥ adṛṣṭena — never seen externally; puruṣa-pravṛtti-rahitam ilāvṛta-vanam — the Ilāvṛta forest inaccessible to ordinary men; okaḥ yasya tena śambhunā — Śambhu whose abode is there.
36.translation: What use are gods who are heroes only in safe places, boasting of prowess away from actual battle? If Kaṁsa objects that he fears Hari and Śambhu, the ministers answer that Hari remains hidden, having entered within everyone and not appearing openly, while Śambhu dwells in the remote Ilāvṛta forest where ordinary men do not go.

37.word_for_word: yadi api — although; udyamaiḥ devāḥ na kiñcid api kartum samarthāḥ — the gods are unable to accomplish anything by their efforts; tathā api — nevertheless; nītiḥ anusartavyā — sound policy must be followed; tathā api iti āhuḥ — therefore they say ‘nevertheless.’
37.translation: Although the gods may be incapable of accomplishing anything by their own efforts, the ministers say that proper political strategy must nevertheless be followed and an enemy must not be ignored.

38.word_for_word: rūḍha-padaḥ — one who has gained a firm position; baddha-mūlaḥ — one whose roots have become firmly fixed.
38.translation: ‘Rūḍha-pada’ means an enemy who has gained a firm position; ‘baddha-mūla’ means one whose roots have become firmly established.

39.word_for_word: devānām mūlam viṣṇuḥ — Viṣṇu is the root of the gods; saḥ ca yatra dharmaḥ tatra āste — and He abides wherever eternal dharma is found; dharmasya mūlam vedādayaḥ — the Vedas and the other sacred foundations are the root of dharma.
39.translation: Viṣṇu is the root of the gods, and He is present wherever eternal dharma is established. The Vedas and the other sacred foundations are in turn the root of that dharma.

42.word_for_word: viprādayaḥ — the brāhmaṇas and the others just named; hareḥ eva tanavaḥ — are indeed the bodies or manifestations of Hari; yasmāt — because this is so; tasmāt ayam eva upāyaḥ — therefore this very course is the means; ayam iti — this is the point of the verses beginning ‘this’; śrīdhara-gloss 42-44 — Śrīdhara marks this single explanation as covering verses 42–44.
42.translation: The brāhmaṇas, cows, Vedas, austerity and the other sacred principles just named are described as the very bodies or manifestations of Hari. Therefore the ministers conclude that attacking these is the direct means of attacking Viṣṇu. Śrīdhara marks this gloss as covering verses 42–44.

43.word_for_word: viprādayaḥ hareḥ eva tanavaḥ — the brāhmaṇas and the other sacred principles are Hari’s own bodies or manifestations; tasmāt ayam eva upāyaḥ — therefore this is the very means; 42-44 — this gloss continues across verses 42–44.
43.translation: This verse continues Śrīdhara’s single gloss on 42–44: because the brāhmaṇas and the other sacred principles are Hari’s own manifestations, the demons regard their destruction as the means to strike at Him.

44.word_for_word: viprādayaḥ hareḥ eva tanavaḥ — the brāhmaṇas and the other sacred principles are Hari’s own manifestations; tasmāt ayam eva upāyaḥ — therefore this is the very means; 42-44 — Śrīdhara’s range-gloss ends here; na vyākhyātam — the following narrative statement itself receives no separate additional explanation.
44.translation: Śrīdhara’s range-gloss on verses 42–44 ends with the demons’ conclusion that persecuting the sages and other sacred foundations is their means of attacking Hari. He gives no separate additional explanation to the narrative statement that follows.

45.word_for_word: ārāt — near, close at hand; samīpam — nearby; āgataḥ mṛtyuḥ yeṣām — those whose death has drawn near.
45.translation: ‘Ārād āgata-mṛtyavaḥ’ means those whose death had already drawn near.
